frameworks.name: Three-Market Segmentation for Athletic Training
frameworks.definition: Athletic training services have three distinct buyer segments with different willingness-to-pay: elite/young athletes (driven by scholarship investment), semi-professional/youth (driven by parental investment in status and skills), and recreational adult athletes (driven by social status and improvement).

claims.text: Young athletes (high school and below) whose parents see training as an investment toward college athletic scholarships pay $300-500/month for specialized coaching (pitching, jumping, hockey) because parents perceive it as a direct path to full-ride tuition, not as a discretionary fitness expense. Alex Hormozi, speaking to a caller exploring athletic training offers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: High school and below competitive athletes
Parents perceive scholarship pathway as realistic
Specialized coaching in high-value sports (pitching, jumping, hockey)
claims.mechanism: Parents frame the expense as college tuition investment, not discretionary spending, shifting the evaluation from price-sensitivity to ROI-on-scholarship-probability.
bounded_by: Does not apply to amateur adult athletes without scholarship pathway
Assumes parents have disposable income to fund training

claims.text: Amateur athletes do not categorically lack disposable income to pay for training; the real constraint is whether the specific service offering (especially remote training) delivers perceived value worth paying for. The market constraint is on perceived value alignment, not income availability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service offering is training delivery (remote or in-person)
claims.mechanism: Buyers perceive value based on service format (remote vs. in-person), not on income category. Misalignment between delivery format and perceived utility is the true constraint, not buyer income.
bounded_by: Does not address absolute poverty constraint
Assumes alternative market segments exist who would pay for the same service

claims.text: A content strategy for athletic training communities that combines champion mindset philosophy with breakdown analysis of real games/fights (paused to explain decision-making, technique, positioning) teaches athletes how to think like champions and creates deeper learning than generic fitness instruction. Alex Hormozi, describing what he would recommend to a UFC executive building a training community.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Target audience is athletes learning sport-specific skills
Content includes both philosophy and tactical breakdown
claims.mechanism: Pause-and-explain breakdowns teach athletes the cognition behind champion decisions, not just the movement, deepening engagement and perceived expertise of the instructor.
bounded_by: Does not apply to fitness-only content without sport-specific context
Requires instructor credibility in the sport being analyzed

claims.text: Recreational adult athletes in organized leagues (softball, basketball, football) represent an undertapped market segment that pays for training to improve performance and maintain social status among peers. Adult league participation has grown substantially in the US, creating demand for coaching that helps players perform better and avoid looking bad in front of friends.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Organized team sports (softball, basketball, football, etc.)
claims.mechanism: Social comparison and desire to maintain peer status drives willingness to pay for skill improvement in recreational contexts, even without professional or scholarship incentives.
bounded_by: Does not apply to solo fitness pursuits
Requires league or team context for peer comparison dynamic

claims.text: A $67 ebook selling training/coaching content can generate approximately $4 million annual revenue at scale, as evidenced by Jacob Hillier's jump training product on YouTube. This demonstrates that low-priced, high-volume content products can achieve significant revenue without high-ticket coaching.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: Product price point to annual revenue

bounded_by: Single data point; may not be reproducible
Assumes similar traffic and conversion as Hillier's YouTube following

examples.text: Jacob Hillier sold a $67 jump training ebook on YouTube and achieved approximately $4 million annual revenue from that single product alone. This demonstrates that specialized athletic training content at a low price point can reach massive scale and revenue when distributed via social platforms with existing audience.

High school athletes pursuing basketball, baseball, or hockey scholarships pay their parents $300-500/month for specialized coaching (e.g., pitching coaches for baseball, jump coaches for basketball) because parents view this as a direct investment in college tuition. This is categorically different from discretionary fitness spending because the ROI is framed as a full-ride scholarship pathway.

A UFC executive exploring a community product asked Hormozi how to structure it. Hormozi recommended building content around the champion's mindset and decision-making philosophy, combined with breakdowns of real fights or games where the champion pauses to explain their tactical choices, positioning, and reasoning. This combination teaches athletes how champions think, not just how they move.

practices.text: When targeting athletic training offers, test multiple buyer segments (competitive youth, amateur hobbyists, recreational adults in leagues) rather than assuming a single niche is the only market. Each segment has different willingness-to-pay and value drivers.

For community or training products aimed at athletes, include both a philosophical or mindset component (e.g., 'how champions think') and tactical breakdowns of real game footage or fight footage to build depth and teachability.
